name: The Bystander Effect
statement: The more people who witness an emergency, the less likely any one of them helps.
statementAccent: the less likely any one of them helps
meaning: Individuals are less likely to help a victim when other people are present, and the more bystanders there are, the less likely any single one is to act, and the slower help tends to come. Responsibility feels shared out among the crowd, so it can end up carried by no one. This is the classic formulation, though the real-world picture, as later work shows, is more favourable to bystanders.
mechanism: Three processes are cited. Diffusion of responsibility means each person feels less personal obligation to act when others could, assuming someone else will. Pluralistic ignorance means people read others' outward calm as a sign the situation is not really an emergency, so each concludes it is not serious. Evaluation apprehension means fear of embarrassment for overreacting or intervening wrongly in front of others. Together these inhibit action, and more strongly as the group grows.

examples.text: Participants alone usually reported smoke seeping into a room within minutes, but in groups with unreactive others most kept working and never reported it — pluralistic ignorance suppressing action.

People who believed they alone heard someone having a seizure over an intercom almost all responded quickly, while those who thought several others were also listening responded far less and more slowly — diffusion of responsibility at work.

examples.tag: Real streets tell a different story
examples.text: Analysis of hundreds of actual public conflicts on CCTV found that in more than nine cases in ten at least one bystander intervened, and more bystanders meant more help — reversing the classic prediction.

variants.name: Diffusion of responsibility
variants.text: The core sub-mechanism and a standalone concept: the sense of personal obligation to act is divided among all those present, so each feels less of it.

variants.name: The Genovese syndrome
variants.text: A colloquial name for the effect, drawn from the Kitty Genovese case — though because that case was badly misreported, the label is tied to a partly mythologised event.

whyItMatters: It is a landmark of social psychology, shaping how emergencies, bystander training, and prosocial behaviour are understood. But it is also a cautionary tale about how a vivid, misreported anecdote can drive a field and enter popular culture, and about the importance of checking laboratory narratives against real-world evidence.

working.text: if you need help in a crowd, point to one person and ask them directly, defeating the diffusion of responsibility.
as a witness, state plainly that this is an emergency, so others do not read your calm as a sign nothing is wrong.
recognise that in real public conflicts people usually do intervene, so the classic dispiriting version overstates inaction.

limits: The effect is a real, replicable laboratory phenomenon under specific conditions — ambiguous, non-dangerous emergencies among strangers — but its popular version is overstated, and its founding anecdote was false. The story of thirty-eight witnesses who watched Kitty Genovese die and did nothing is unsupported by the evidence; there is no basis for the number, and at least one witness shouted at the attacker. Real-world CCTV analysis finds bystanders intervene in the great majority of public conflicts, and the effect attenuates or reverses in clearly dangerous emergencies. It is best seen as genuine under narrow conditions, wrapped in an exaggerated narrative.
misreadings: It does not show that crowds reliably fail to help — in real recorded emergencies, intervention is the norm, and more bystanders can mean more help. And the Kitty Genovese story that inspired it is largely a myth, so it should be cited as the misreported case that sparked the research, not as fact.
origin: Formalised by John Darley and Bibb Latane in two 1968 experiments, prompted by the misreported 1964 murder of Kitty Genovese; the exaggerations in that story were documented by Manning, Levine, and Collins in 2007.

sources.text: Bystander effect, Wikipedia. — the definition, the mechanisms, the 1968 experiments, and the Genovese myth and Philpot real-world findings.
Manning, Levine & Collins, "The Kitty Genovese murder and the social psychology of helping," American Psychologist 62(6):555-562 (2007), PubMed.
